questions.prompt: 1 of 3 · Simultaneous start — You and Avery start speaking together. You have spoken often; Avery has not.

options.feedback: Not quite. This risks dominating someone with fewer turns.

options.text: “Go ahead, Avery. I have a related point to share afterward.”
options.feedback: Good choice. This supports participation while preserving your opportunity.

options.text: Say your idea is more important.
options.feedback: Not quite. This creates unnecessary conflict.

questions.prompt: 2 of 3 · Direct response — Jordan raises a concern your research addresses, but someone else also wants to speak.

options.text: “Could I respond briefly with a relevant finding, then hear the next perspective?”
options.feedback: Good choice. This explains the connection and acknowledges others.

options.text: Ignore them and speak at length.
options.feedback: Not quite. Relevant research still needs collaborative delivery.

options.text: Never speak if anyone else wants a turn.
options.feedback: Not quite. Withholding useful evidence can hinder the group.

questions.prompt: 3 of 3 · Cut off mid-sentence — Your voice fades and another student begins before you finish.

options.feedback: Not quite. Escalation does not resolve the speaking order.

options.text: “I’d like to finish this thought, then hear your point.” Finish briefly and yield.
options.feedback: Good choice. This preserves your turn while respecting the other speaker.
